problem: Federated audio models leave most recordings unused when only a small fraction of local clips have labels.
contribution: FedSTAR learns jointly from labels and confidence-filtered pseudo-labels, with optional self-supervised initialization to improve early convergence.
reading_guide: First compare equal label budgets, then check the class-distribution assumption and the separate effect of model initialization.

diagram.title: Learn locally, aggregate, repeat
diagram.description: The server broadcasts model weights. Each client jointly trains on labeled clips and confident pseudo-labels from unlabeled clips, then returns weights for FedAvg and the next round.

stages.title: Broadcast model
stages.detail: Send the current shared weights to the clients selected for this round.

stages.title: Local self-training
stages.detail: Jointly optimize labeled clips and pseudo-labels that pass the changing confidence threshold.

stages.title: Aggregate updates
stages.detail: Average returned model parameters to create the next shared model.

diagram.footnote: FedAvg returns the aggregated model to the next broadcast. Optional FSD-50K contrastive pretraining initializes this cycle; it is separate from the local self-training procedure.

results.title: Learning with 3% labels
results.question: Does unlabeled audio help when the supervised baseline receives exactly the same labeled clips?
results.context: 15 clients; 3% labels, remaining clips available unlabeled; 100 rounds, one local epoch, 80% participation, data-distribution variance 25%, unlabeled-loss weight 0.5. Mean test accuracy (%) over three runs; higher is better.
results.interpretation: FedSTAR improves each of these three task-specific comparisons, with a much larger gap on Speech Commands than on VoxForge.
results.caveat: The appendix prints ± values and calls them variance across experiments; they are retained verbatim, with no conversion to standard deviations or confidence intervals. These rows share a client count and label budget, but represent different tasks; their accuracies should not be pooled.

results.title: Labeled classes missing locally
results.question: Can unlabeled examples help when clients have labels for only a few classes?
results.context: Speech Commands; 15 clients, 3% labels, mean of three labeled classes per client out of 12; unlabeled clips are randomly distributed and may cover all classes. 100 rounds, one local epoch, 80% participation. Mean test accuracy (%), higher is better.
results.interpretation: Unlabeled coverage supplies information absent from each client’s labeled subset, giving large gains in this particular distribution experiment.
results.caveat: The appendix prints ± values and calls them variance across experiments; they are retained verbatim, with no conversion to standard deviations or confidence intervals. This does not test the case where both labeled and unlabeled client data lack the same classes.

results.title: Pretraining after 100 rounds
results.question: Does a better initialization always give a higher final accuracy?
results.context: Speech Commands; 15 clients, 50% of the remaining unlabeled pool used; label budget varies by row. 100 rounds, one local epoch, 80% participation. Mean test accuracy (%) over three runs; higher is better.
results.interpretation: At this fixed unlabeled budget, pretraining helps the 20% and 50% label settings but does not improve the two smaller label budgets after 100 rounds.
results.caveat: The appendix prints ± values and calls them variance across experiments; they are retained verbatim, with no conversion to standard deviations or confidence intervals. This endpoint comparison is distinct from Figure 6’s early-convergence experiment at 10 rounds.

evaluation.label: Data
evaluation.value: Ambient Acoustic Contexts (10 events), Speech Commands v2 (12 classes), VoxForge (6 languages); FSD-50K for optional contrastive pretraining.

evaluation.label: Models
evaluation.value: Four-block convolutional audio network using log-mel inputs, group normalization and spatial dropout.

evaluation.label: Compared with
evaluation.value: Centralized supervised training and supervised FedAvg with matching local labeled subsets; random versus pretrained FedSTAR.

evaluation.label: Protocol
evaluation.value: Flower simulations with 5–30 clients, 20–80% participation, 1–4 local epochs and three full runs per setting.

limitations: Self-training needs some reliable labels and assumes local labeled and unlabeled audio come from the same distribution.
The strongest class-skew gains use unlabeled data that may contain all classes even where labeled data do not.
More local training can harm the 3% label setting through overfitting or incorrect pseudo-labels; benefits are not universal across configurations.
Experiments simulate federated clients. Real-device energy, system heterogeneity and formal differential privacy are not established.
takeaways: Keeping unlabeled audio in the training loop can be more useful than discarding it when local labels are scarce.
Optional public-data pretraining improves early learning in many settings, but its final-accuracy benefit depends on the label budget.
The distribution of unlabeled examples is part of the result, not an incidental implementation detail.

evidence_inventory.version: ACM TECS 21(6), Article 74, 2022; final publisher PDF with repository cover and appendix (27 PDF pages).
